Services

Trust setup and annual returns

A discretionary trust separates who controls the assets from who receives the income. Setting one up is a deed, a trustee and a short list of registrations. Keeping it out of trouble is a resolution signed every 30 June, and a return lodged after it.

Get a fixed-fee quoteNo obligation — one price in writing, usually within one business day.

Our fee

from $649 fixed, inc. GST

Fixed, agreed in writing, no work begins before you accept it.

Government charges

Varies by state

Duty on the trust deed applies in some states and not others. We tell you the figure for yours before you commit. A corporate trustee adds an ASIC registration fee.

Who does it

A registered tax agent

BRS Advisory Pty Ltd, Registered Tax Agent, CPA Australia Public Practice. Every client ID-verified before work starts.

What’s included

  • The structure question first — whether a trust helps you, or just adds a return you now have to lodge
  • Trust deed prepared and executed, with the trustee, appointor and beneficiary class set out
  • A corporate trustee registered with ASIC where that is the better answer
  • TFN and ABN for the trust, and GST registration where turnover calls for it
  • Annual financial statements and the trust tax return
  • Distribution resolutions drafted and signed before 30 June, every year
  • Each beneficiary’s own return matched to what the trust actually distributed

How it runs

  1. 01 Verify identity online — each director, trustee or controlling owner does a three-minute check on their phone, included in the fee. Every client, every service, no exceptions. How it works.
  2. 02 Tell us who needs to control the assets and who should receive the income — they are rarely the same person.
  3. 03 The deed is prepared and executed, stamped where your state requires it, and the trustee is put in place.
  4. 04 Registrations go in — TFN, ABN, and GST if the turnover calls for it.
  5. 05 Each year we prepare the accounts, draft the resolution before 30 June, and lodge the return after it.

The part that catches people

If no beneficiary is presently entitled to the trust’s income as at 30 June, the trustee is assessed on it instead — and that may be at the top rate of tax. It is a signature on a date, and missing it is the most expensive clerical error in the structure.

The other one is distributions that exist only on paper. Where income is allocated to an adult child or a related entity but the money goes somewhere else, the ATO looks at it under the reimbursement agreement rules in section 100A. We would rather set the distribution up so the question never arises.

Unit trusts, when the owners need fixed shares

A discretionary trust is the standard choice for a family. Where the people involved are not family — two business partners, or two households buying a property together — a unit trust usually fits better. Each owner holds units, and income and capital follow the units, much like shares in a company. The trustee has no discretion over who receives what.

Setting one up follows the same steps: a deed, a trustee (often a company, so no individual holds the assets personally), the first issue of units recorded in a unit register, then the TFN, ABN and GST registrations. We also recommend a unitholders’ agreement covering what happens when someone wants out.

Two things to know before you start. Some states charge duty on the deed or on later transfers of units, particularly where the trust holds land, and the land tax treatment differs from state to state. We give you the figures for your state, alongside our fixed fee, before anything is signed.

Work the numbers first

  • Capital gains tax

    What a sale inside the trust costs, including the discount where the asset has been held long enough.

  • Rental property

    Rent, interest and depreciation netted off, for property held in a trust or in your own name.

A real practice, not a form that emails you a PDF
